result: The authors performed scRNAseq on 4 dpf larval zebrafish spinal cords, sequencing approximately 10,000-15,000 cells per replicate to a depth of 40,000 reads per cell. After quality control, 11,762 spinal cord cells were analyzed, yielding 30 clusters, of which 27 were identifiable as neuronal or glial based on established markers.
evaluation: All reviewers accepted the experimental design and clustering approach without critique. Reviewers noted the work 'builds on a strong foundation of literature' and that 'well-established neuronal markers allow the transcriptomic analyses to match a majority of the transcriptomic clusters to specific spinal neuron subtypes.'

result: The neuronal population was reclustered into 33 clusters and assigned identities using a combination code based on neurotransmitter biosynthesis/transporter genes and differentially expressed markers. This yielded four principal neurotransmitter categories (glutamatergic, glycinergic, GABAergic, cholinergic), with 22 of 33 clusters confidently assigned to known cell types. The relative abundance of cell types was consistent with published in vivo labeling experiments.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the classification approach, noting that 'well-established neuronal markers allow the transcriptomic analyses to match a majority of the transcriptomic clusters to specific spinal neuron subtypes' and that results are 'optimally placed in the context of the rich background and literature regarding zebrafish spinal neuron physiology.'

result: The authors identified molecular markers distinguishing v2a interneuron subtypes (type I vs. type II), including differential expression of vsx2, shox2, and a newly identified marker gjd2b for type II v2a neurons. These assignments were validated by in situ hybridization showing gjd2b colocalization with weakly fluorescent v2a neurons in Tg(vsx2:Kaede) fish.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the v2a subtype identification or the gjd2b marker discovery. The validation experiments were accepted without comment, indicating implicit support for these findings.

result: The authors claim that type II v2a interneurons are recruited more effectively across the range of high swimming speeds compared to type I, citing previous functional studies.
evaluation: One reviewer explicitly disagreed with this interpretation, stating 'Both Type I and Type II V2a neurons are recruited during very fast swimming (70 Hz). The degree of the de-recruitment of Type I V2a neurons during slower swimming (40-60 Hz) is larger than Type II. Thus...Type I V2a neurons are more analogous to PMns than Type II V2a neurons.' The authors chose not to modify the manuscript despite this critique.

result: The authors identified chromogranin A (chga) as a novel marker for CoLo interneurons, validated by in situ hybridization showing one large neuron per hemi-segment in the appropriate rostral location, and confirmed by co-labeling with GFP-labeled CoLo neurons based on morphology.
evaluation: Reviewers did not question the CoLo identification or chga marker validation. The finding was implicitly accepted as part of the broader validation of interneuron types.

result: The authors identified pnoca (encoding Prepronociceptin) as a highly specific marker for DoLA interneurons, validated by in situ hybridization and morphological characterization showing long ascending axons with short ventral projections. They speculate that DoLAs may function as neuropeptide-releasing neurons modulating sensory functions.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the DoLA identification or pnoca marker specificity. The morphological validation was accepted without comment. The speculative functional interpretation was not critiqued.

result: The authors identified a cholinergic interneuron cluster expressing evx1/evx2 but lacking motor neuron markers, representing the zebrafish homolog of mammalian v0c interneurons. These neurons differ from mouse v0c by coexpressing glutamatergic markers. Morphological characterization showed soma near the dorsal motor column boundary with long descending processes (>6 segments) and bouton-like enlargements near motor neuron soma.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly noted that 'one transcriptomic cluster reveals the presence in zebrafish of a spinal neuron subtype previously identified in mammals,' affirming this discovery. The morphological and molecular characterization was not challenged.

result: Motor neurons comprised ~27% of neuronal transcriptomes (1354 cells from whole spinal cord). FACS-sorted motor neurons yielded 7790 additional cells (>92% purity). Integration produced 9144 motor neurons in 10 clusters, including a small cluster (3.6%) expressing gfra1a/tbx3b that may represent non-skeletal muscle motor neurons similar to those in mouse.
evaluation: Reviewers did not question the motor neuron isolation strategy or the identification of the small non-skeletal muscle motor neuron cluster. The integration of FACS-sorted and computationally isolated populations was accepted without critique.

result: The authors identified chga as a specific marker for primary motor neurons (PMns) and nr2f1a for secondary motor neurons (SMns), validated by in situ hybridization showing segregated dorsal (large, chga+) vs. ventral (smaller, nr2f1a+) distributions. Co-labeling confirmed chga expression in all PMn types (CaP, MiP, RoP). Cell counts showed ~18-fold more SMns than PMns, consistent with previous studies.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed this finding, noting that the work 'discovered molecular distinctions causally related to the unique physiology of primary motoneuron (PMn) function.' The validation experiments were not challenged.

result: The authors subdivided SMns into three groups based on differential expression of foxb1b, alcamb, and bmp16, representing ~95% of SMns. These markers showed distinct dorsal-ventral distributions, validated by co-labeling with transgenic lines. They speculate that bmp16+ motor neurons may innervate slow muscle.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the SMn subtype classification or marker validation. The speculative connection to slow muscle innervation was not critiqued.

result: Differential expression analysis identified 508 genes distinguishing PMns from SMns (317 higher in PMns). GO enrichment revealed PMn-specific enrichment in synaptic function, ion channels, and ATP generation categories. PMns showed enrichment of 29 synaptic genes and 8 ion channel subunits, while SMns showed no specific enrichment in these categories but high levels of transcription factors and RNA binding proteins (118/191 enriched genes).
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed this finding, stating the authors 'discovered, in the motor neurons of the escape circuit, two functional groups or "cassettes" of genes related to excitability and vesicle release, respectively.' The differential expression analysis was not challenged.

result: The authors identified an ion channel cassette (cacna1ab, scn4ba, kcnc3a) coexpressed in >55% of PMns but <3% of SMns. In situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry validated specific expression in PMns. CaP ablation experiments showed specific reduction of Kcnc3 antibody staining in ventral muscle synapses, confirming PMn-specific expression.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed this as a key finding, noting 'compelling evidence that PMNs, and two types of interneurons innervating them, express a set of three genes encoding voltage-gated ion channels enabling rapid firing.' The validation experiments were not challenged.

result: The ion channel and synaptic cassettes identified in PMns are also highly expressed in type II v2a and CoLo interneurons compared to other interneuron types. The scn4ba sodium channel β subunit is the strongest delineator for cassette classification. Synaptic proteins (vamp1a/b, syt2a/b, snap25a, stxbp1a, cplx2l) show similar enrichment patterns.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly noted this finding, stating 'the primary motor neuron and specific interneurons of the circuit mediating strong and fast swimming share expression of cassettes of ion channel and synapse-related gene cassette that sculpt fast and strong synaptic transmission.' This was identified as a key contribution.

result: The authors conclude that PMns express functional cassettes of ion channels and synaptic proteins specialized for high-frequency firing and augmented transmitter release, contributing to greater power generation during escape and fast swimming. These cassettes are shared with specific interneurons in the escape circuit.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed this as the central finding, noting 'they defined functional "cassettes" comprising specific combinations of voltage-dependent ion channel types and synaptic proteins, likely responsible for generating maximal motor outputs.' One reviewer stated 'this finding will be important to the field.'

result: The authors interpret the functional significance of the ion channel cassette based on previous literature: cacna1ab (P/Q-type calcium channel) mediates high release probability; scn4ba (β4 sodium channel subunit) enables high-frequency firing; kcnc3a (Kv3.3 potassium channel) promotes fast repolarization. They note this cassette is conserved in mammalian fast-signaling neurons (calyx of Held, pyramidal neurons).
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the functional interpretation, noting 'the ion channel and synapse-related gene cassettes that distinguish the primary motor neuron circuit are shared with some mammalian circuits that also generate fast, reliable synaptic transmission.' The mechanistic interpretation based on literature was not challenged.

result: The authors cite previous studies showing type II v2a interneurons can fire at high frequencies (>600 Hz) and note that fast motor neurons are selectively vulnerable in ALS.
evaluation: These citations were not challenged by reviewers and serve as contextual support for the functional significance of the cassette findings.
